newsitem.title: FRANCE: Jobless dip gives French government poll boost.
newsitem.headline: Jobless dip gives French government poll boost.

text.p: France's centre-right government got a campaign boost on Wednesday when the last unemployment figures to be released before next month's general election showed a slight dip in the giant jobless total.

Unemployment fell by 4,800 to 3,087,500 in March, according to national criteria, although the jobless rate calculated on International Labour Organisation (ILO) rules remained at the record 12.8 percent of the workforce it reached in February.

It was the second monthly pinprick in a row in joblessness, shown by polls to be the voters' number one concern in the run-up to the May 25-June 1 snap National Assembly election. The total dipped 7,500 in February.

Conservative Prime Minister Alain Juppe, whose popularity has sunk as unemployment has risen from 11.7 percent when he took office in 1995, said the March figures showed the rise in unemployment had stopped.

The Socialist opposition denounced the figures as drastically understating the extent of the jobs crisis. The International Monetary Fund forecast last week that France's jobless rate would rise above 13 percent this year.

President Jacques Chirac, trying to nudge voters to the centre-right, said the coalition should give top priority if it wins re-election to a bill to fight poverty by creating 300,000 minimum-wage jobs and building subsidised housing.

National Assembly debate on the bill was suspended on April 21 when Chirac called the early elections, saying France needed a new impulse partly to join a single European currency in 1999 from a position of strength.
Government spokesman Alain Lamassoure quoted Chirac as telling the cabinet that a draft farm bill would strengthen French agricultural exports and ensure domestic supplies.

On the left, the opposition Socialists and tiny Greens party, battling polls indicating the government is likely to retain power, agreed on joint candidates in about a sixth of constituencies as part of a left-wing unity drive.

"For the first time in their history, the Greens will be able to enter the National Assembly," Greens leader Dominique Voynet predicted at a joint news conference with Socialist Party leader Lionel Jospin.

Under the deal, a Greens candidate would represent the Socialists in 29 constituencies while the Socialist candidate in 77 constituencies would also represent the Greens and the tiny Radical party. The National Assembly has 577 seats.

Jospin accuses Chirac of calling the rushed election to try to stifle debate about the government's record -- such as on jobs -- and says Juppe's coalition is planning a further bout of austerity to help qualify for the euro common currency.

French unemployment is the highest in the Group of Seven major industrial democracies, although the country has a forest of job-creation subsidies and work experience programmes. The next monthly jobless figures are not due to be published until June 2, a day after the election runoff.

Juppe got bad news from an opinion poll showing his popularity had dipped to match last year's all-time low. The CSA survey showed he won a favourable rating from just 28 percent, down two points from March, with 65 percent against.
Forty-one percent expressed support for Chirac, up from 36 percent, with 55 percent against.

Left and right have set out sharply differing approaches to creating jobs in their election platforms. The centre-right coalition has stressed curbing public spending, cutting payroll charges on the low paid, negotiating more flexible working hours and slimming down the civil service.

The Socialist and Communist parties pledged on Tuesday to create 700,000 jobs for young people, half of them in the public sector, legislate to reduce the work week gradually to 35 hours from 39 and take measures to boost wages and consumer demand.
